```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 300)
options(knitr.kable.NA = "–")
library(ggplot2)
res <- function(f) utils::read.csv(file.path("results", f), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
pit <- res("pitfalls.csv")
val <- res("validation.csv")
vbr <- res("validation_by_round.csv")
deff <- res("design_effects.csv")
qual <- res("quality.csv")
syn <- res("synthetic_fidelity.csv")
syn_d <- res("synthetic_fidelity_detail.csv")
trend <- res("case_csection_trend.csv")
chg <- res("case_csection_changes.csv")
ineq <- res("case_csection_inequality.csv")
dec <- res("case_csection_decomposition.csv")
sdg <- res("sdg.csv")

f1 <- function(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
n_val <- nrow(val)
n_pass <- sum(val$pass)
med_diff <- stats::median(abs(val$computed - val$official))
cs <- trend[trend$indicator == "rh_del_csection", ]
fd <- trend[trend$indicator == "rh_del_facility", ]
cs_at <- function(s) cs$estimate[cs$survey_id == s]
fd_at <- function(s) fd$estimate[fd$survey_id == s]
iq <- function(s, m, col = "estimate") ineq[ineq$survey_id == s & ineq$measure == m, col]
dc <- function(from, by, comp, col = "estimate") dec[dec$from == from & dec$by == by & dec$component == comp, col]
ch <- function(i, a, b, col) chg[chg$indicator == i & chg$survey_1 == a & chg$survey_2 == b, col]
p <- function(name, survey, col = "naive", group = NULL) {
  r <- pit[pit$pitfall == name & pit$survey_id == survey, ]
  if (!is.null(group)) r <- r[r$group == group, ]
  r[[col]][1]
}
qv <- function(s, col) qual[[col]][qual$survey_id == s]
n_margins <- sum(syn$margins)
yr4 <- function(x) sub("^BD(\\d{4})DHS$", "\\1", x)
```

Arman Hossen^1^

^1^ Department of Statistics, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, USA

Corresponding author: Arman Hossen, hossena@miamioh.edu, ORCID 0009-0003-4346-1026

# Abstract

**Background:** The Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) has been
run nine times since 1993 and is the main source of population and health
statistics for the country. Secondary analyses of the respondent-level files
are common, but they are rarely checked against the officially published
estimates, and several features of the survey design are easy to get wrong.

**Methods:** We built bdhs, an open-source R package covering every BDHS
round from 1993-94 to 2022. It bundles all official estimates published
through the DHS Program and provides tools for the licensed microdata: file
identification, cross-round harmonisation, complex survey designs, 97
indicator definitions, fertility and mortality rates, data-quality
diagnostics, and inequality, trend and decomposition analysis. We also
developed a method for generating synthetic BDHS data calibrated to the
official estimates. We recomputed every indicator with a published value from
the original recode files, quantified the effect of common analytic errors,
and assessed data quality across rounds.

**Results:** Of `r n_val` national estimates computed across eight rounds,
`r n_pass` matched the official value (median absolute difference
`r f1(med_diff, 2)` percentage points). Ignoring the short women's
questionnaire used in 2022 reduced unmet need for family planning from
`r f1(p("2022 short questionnaire ignored", "BD2022DHS", "correct"))`% to
`r f1(p("2022 short questionnaire ignored", "BD2022DHS"))`%, and treating the
ever-married sample as all women inflated child marriage by about ten
percentage points. Design effects of `r f1(min(deff$deff))` to
`r f1(max(deff$deff))` meant that ignoring the sample design made standard
errors up to `r f1(sqrt(max(deff$deff)))` times too small. Data quality
improved over time, although height-for-age z-scores remained more dispersed
than expected and ages at death were heaped at 12 months. Synthetic data
reproduced `r format(n_margins, big.mark = ",")` official national and
subnational values with a maximum deviation of `r f1(max(syn$max_abs_diff), 2)`
percentage points.

**Conclusions:** BDHS analyses can reproduce the official estimates almost
exactly, but only when the sampling frame, questionnaire changes and survey
design are handled correctly. Validated open-source tools make such analyses
faster and easier to check, and calibrated synthetic data allow methods to be
taught and shared without the restricted files.

**Keywords:** Demographic and Health Surveys; Bangladesh; complex survey
design; reproducibility; validation; synthetic data; health inequality; R

# Background

Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) provide much of what is known about
fertility, family planning, maternal and child health and nutrition in low-
and middle-income countries. Bangladesh has taken part since the early 1990s
and has now completed nine rounds: 1993-94, 1996-97, 1999-2000, 2004, 2007,
2011, 2014, 2017-18 and 2022. The surveys are carried out by the National
Institute of Population Research and Training (NIPORT) with technical
assistance from ICF [@niport2024]. Official estimates appear in the final
reports and through the DHS Program's online tools, while the
respondent-level files are released to registered researchers.

These files support a large secondary literature, yet published estimates
from them are seldom compared with the official figures. When they differ,
readers cannot tell whether the difference is substantive or simply a
computational slip. The definitions in the Guide to DHS Statistics
[@croft2018] are clear, but applying them to Bangladesh requires attention to
details that are not visible in the data files. The women's samples are
restricted to women who have ever been married, so indicators for all women
need adjustment factors. Division boundaries and codes changed three times
between rounds. The 2022 survey gave a third of women a shortened
questionnaire. Some questions are specific to Bangladesh and do not belong in
the standard definitions. An error at any of these points carries through to
the published result without warning.

Several tools already help with parts of this work. The rdhs package gives
access to the DHS Program's data and indicator services [@watson2019],
DHS.rates computes fertility and childhood mortality rates [@dhsrates], the
survey package implements design-based estimation [@lumley2004], and
IPUMS-DHS distributes harmonised extracts of selected variables across
countries [@ipumsdhs]. What is missing is a way to check an analysis of the
original files against the official estimates, a record of the
country-specific decisions this requires, and a way to share reproducible
analyses when the data themselves cannot be shared.

This paper introduces bdhs, an R package [@rcore] for all BDHS rounds, and
uses it to answer four questions. How closely can the official estimates be
reproduced from the recode files? How much do common analytic errors change
the results? What does a systematic data-quality assessment show across
rounds? And can synthetic data reproduce the published estimates closely
enough to be useful for teaching and method development? We illustrate the
analytic tools with the rise of caesarean delivery between 2004 and 2022.

# Methods

## Data

The package bundles all `r format(310528, big.mark = ",")` official estimates
published for Bangladesh through the DHS Program's indicator service, covering
every indicator, round and breakdown. It also bundles the definitions of 2,607
indicators, catalogues of the 13 Bangladesh surveys and their 441 data files,
codebooks with variable names and labels but no respondent values, and the
division boundaries used in each survey. No respondent-level data are
distributed, in line with the DHS terms of use.

The analyses in this paper used the author's licensed copies of the recode
files: the children's recode for 1993-94, 1999-2000, 2004, 2007, 2011, 2014,
2017-18 and 2022; the births, household, women's and household-member
recodes for 2017-18; and the women's and household-member recodes for 2022.
Only aggregate results are reported, and the analysis scripts are publicly
available.

## The bdhs package

bdhs identifies DHS files by their names or, for renamed files, by their
contents, and keeps a fast local copy. It harmonises 112 variables across
rounds using 1,008 round-specific rules. Each rule is checked against the
value labels in the data, so a recoding error raises a warning instead of
passing silently. Survey designs use the DHS sampling-error strata, the
enumeration areas as primary sampling units, and normalised sample weights.
Pooled analyses keep each round's strata and clusters separate and offer
normalised, de-normalised and equal weighting.

Indicators are defined in code. Each definition records the denominator,
reference period, recode file, weight and, where needed, the all-woman factor.
A single function call therefore returns any of the 97 indicators with
design-based standard errors. Fertility and childhood mortality rates use the
DHS synthetic-cohort methods with jackknife standard errors. The package
documentation lists every function.

## Validation

For every indicator with an official value, we computed the national estimate
from each available recode file and compared it with the official value for
the same reference period. A comparison passed if the absolute difference was
no more than 0.5 percentage points (or the equivalent for rates), plus half a
unit of the precision to which the official value is rounded.

## Analytic pitfalls and design effects

Whenever a decision changed a result during validation, we kept both
versions: the estimate a straightforward but naive analysis gives, and the
correct one. Design effects for headline indicators were computed as the
ratio of the design-based variance to the variance under simple random
sampling with the same number of observations.

## Data quality

The data-quality module implements the standard DHS diagnostics
[@pullum2006]. These cover:

- age heaping in the household roster, measured by the Whipple index for ages
  23-62 and by Myers' blended index;
- the ratio of women recorded at age 50 to those at 49, which detects ages
  being shifted at the upper boundary of eligibility for the women's
  interview;
- completeness of birth dates;
- the ratio of births in the fifth year before the survey to those in the
  fourth year, which detects births being displaced out of the window for the
  health questions;
- heaping of reported ages at death at 12 months;
- the dispersion of anthropometric z-scores, the share of flagged values and
  terminal-digit preference in measured height [@who2019anthro].

As in the DHS data-quality tables, these statistics are unweighted.

## Calibrated synthetic data

Synthetic data are generated without access to any microdata, in three steps.

1. **Structure.** A synthetic population is created with the same files,
   variables, codes, labels, clusters, strata and weights as the real survey.
   Its size and its allocation to division-by-residence strata follow the
   official sample sizes and weighted distributions.
2. **Calibration.** For each target indicator (four to seven per recode file,
   for example facility delivery, contraceptive use and child stunting), the
   probability of the outcome in each division-by-residence cell is modelled
   on the logit scale as an intercept plus a division effect and a residence
   effect. These effects are found by iterative proportional fitting
   [@deming1940], so that the weighted national, division and residence
   values equal the official estimates for the indicator's reference period.
3. **Assignment.** Outcomes are assigned deterministically within cells, so
   the calibrated values are reproduced up to rounding rather than up to
   random error. Stratum weights are then raked to the official denominators
   of all targets.

The idea follows fully synthetic data for statistical disclosure limitation
[@rubin1993; @raghunathan2003], with one important difference: it uses only
published aggregates, so the synthetic files contain no information about any
respondent. They reproduce the calibrated values, but not the associations
between indicators or the variables that were not calibrated.

## Trends, inequality and decomposition

Changes between rounds were tested as differences between independent survey
estimates and expressed per year using the midpoints of fieldwork. Within a
round, contrasts between groups used the full design-based covariance matrix.

Inequality by household wealth was measured with:

- the difference and the ratio between the richest and poorest quintiles;
- the slope and relative indices of inequality, estimated by design-based
  regression on the weighted ridit of the wealth quintiles [@barros2013];
- the concentration index [@wagstaff1991; @kakwani1997], and for binary
  outcomes Erreygers' corrected index [@erreygers2009].

Changes between two rounds were split into a part due to shifts in the
composition of mothers and a part due to changes within groups, using
Kitagawa's method with symmetric weights [@kitagawa1955; @dasgupta1993] and
delete-one-cluster jackknife standard errors.

Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) was assessed from
the official estimates by comparing the average annual rate of change since
2014 with the rate needed to reach each 2030 target. Where no numerical SDG
target exists, published benchmarks were used [@fabic2015].

All analyses were done in R [@rcore] with bdhs version 0.1.0 and the survey
package [@lumley2004].

# Results

## Agreement with the official estimates

Of the `r n_val` national estimates we could compute, `r n_pass` matched the
official value (Table 1). The median absolute difference was
`r f1(med_diff, 2)` percentage points, and it was below 0.04 points in every
round. The two estimates that did not match were women's thinness and
overweight in 2022 computed from the women's recode. The DHS Program
calculates these from the household-member recode, which includes all women
in the biomarker subsample rather than only those who have ever been married.
Computed from that file, both match the official values.

```{r tab1}
t1 <- vbr
t1$survey_id <- yr4(t1$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t1, col.names = c("Survey", "Recode files", "Estimates", "Matched",
                               "Median absolute difference", "Largest difference among matches"),
             caption = "Table 1. Agreement between estimates computed with bdhs and the official DHS values (percentage points)")
```

## How much common errors matter

Table 2 shows, for each pitfall we identified, the estimate from a naive
analysis next to the correct estimate. The two largest errors come from the
structure of the sample.

Every BDHS women's sample consists of women who have ever been married.
Analysing it as if it represented all women puts the share of women aged
20-24 who married before 18 at
`r f1(p("Ever-married sample treated as all women", "BD2017DHS"))`% in
2017-18; the correct figure is
`r f1(p("Ever-married sample treated as all women", "BD2017DHS", "correct"))`%.

In 2022, a third of women answered a short questionnaire with no family
planning questions. Counting them as having no unmet need gives
`r f1(p("2022 short questionnaire ignored", "BD2022DHS"))`% instead of
`r f1(p("2022 short questionnaire ignored", "BD2022DHS", "correct"))`%.

The other pitfalls are smaller but still exceed the sampling error:

- counting the country-specific liquids lowers exclusive breastfeeding in
  2007 from
  `r f1(p("Country-specific liquids counted in exclusive breastfeeding", "BD2007DHS", "correct"))`%
  to `r f1(p("Country-specific liquids counted in exclusive breastfeeding", "BD2007DHS"))`%;
- leaving out births to mothers under 15 lowers the general fertility rate;
- ignoring the measles-rubella vaccine lowers measles coverage;
- using the subgroup all-woman factor for child marriage, rather than the
  total factor that the official tables use for every subgroup, shifts the
  urban estimate by
  `r f1(abs(p("Subgroup all-woman factor in child-marriage tables", "BD2017DHS", "correct", "urban") - p("Subgroup all-woman factor in child-marriage tables", "BD2017DHS", "naive", "urban")))`
  points.

Division codes add a trap of a different kind: code 5 means Rajshahi in 2014
but Mymensingh in 2017-18, so comparing codes across rounds compares
different places.

```{r tab2}
t2 <- pit[!is.na(pit$naive), c("pitfall", "survey_id", "group", "naive", "correct", "official")]
t2$survey_id <- yr4(t2$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t2, row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Pitfall", "Survey", "Group", "Naive estimate", "Correct estimate", "Official value"),
             caption = "Table 2. Effect of common analytic errors on BDHS estimates (%)")
```

Design effects for headline indicators ranged from `r f1(min(deff$deff))` to
`r f1(max(deff$deff))` (Table 3). An analysis that treats the survey as a
simple random sample would therefore report confidence intervals up to
`r f1(sqrt(max(deff$deff)))` times too narrow. The largest design effects were
for delivery care, which is strongly clustered by area.

```{r tab3}
t3 <- deff
t3$survey_id <- yr4(t3$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Survey", "Indicator", "Estimate (%)", "SE, design-based", "SE, simple random sample", "Design effect", "n"),
             caption = "Table 3. Design effects for headline indicators")
```

## Data quality

Birth dates were reported almost completely in every round, and we found no
sign of births being shifted out of the five-year window for the health
questions (Table 4). Anthropometric quality improved considerably. Flagged
height-for-age z-scores fell from `r f1(qv("BD2007DHS", "child_haz_pct_flagged"))`%
in 2007 to `r f1(qv("BD2022DHS", "child_haz_pct_flagged"))`% in 2022. Child
heights ending in 0 or 5 fell from
`r f1(qv("BD2000DHS", "child_height_pct_digit_0_or_5"))`% in 1999-2000 to
`r f1(qv("BD2022DHS", "child_height_pct_digit_0_or_5"))`% in 2022, close to the
20% expected without digit preference. Even so, the standard deviation of
height-for-age z-scores stayed between
`r f1(min(qual$child_haz_sd, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` and
`r f1(max(qual$child_haz_sd, na.rm = TRUE), 2)`, above the range of 1.0 to 1.2
expected for good-quality data [@who2019anthro].

Age reporting in the household roster was much less precise for men than for
women. In 2017-18 the Whipple index was `r f1(qv("BD2017DHS", "whipple_men"), 0)`
for men and `r f1(qv("BD2017DHS", "whipple_women"), 0)` for women; 100 means
no heaping and 500 means every age ends in 0 or 5. There were also far fewer
women recorded at 50 than at 49, with a ratio of
`r f1(qv("BD2017DHS", "women_ratio_50_to_49"), 2)` in 2017-18 and
`r f1(qv("BD2022DHS", "women_ratio_50_to_49"), 2)` in 2022 where about 1 would
be expected. Ages at death were heaped at 12 months, with a heaping index of
`r f1(qv("BD2017DHS", "heaping_12_months"), 0)` in 2017-18 (100 means no
heaping).

```{r tab4}
t4 <- qual
t4$survey_id <- yr4(t4$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t4, row.names = FALSE, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Survey", "Birth dates complete (%)", "SD of height-for-age z", "Flagged height-for-age (%)",
                           "Heights ending in 0 or 5 (%)", "Whipple index, men", "Whipple index, women",
                           "Women aged 50 : 49", "Heaping of deaths at 12 months"),
             caption = "Table 4. Data-quality indicators by survey round (unweighted). A dash means the statistic needs a recode file that was not available.")
```

## Calibrated synthetic data

Synthetic files were generated for every round and for the children's,
women's and household-member recodes. Together they reproduced
`r format(n_margins, big.mark = ",")` official national, division and residence
values. The mean absolute deviation per round and file ranged from
`r f1(min(syn$mean_abs_diff), 2)` to `r f1(max(syn$mean_abs_diff), 2)`
percentage points, and the largest single deviation was
`r f1(max(syn$max_abs_diff), 2)` points (Table 5, Figure 1). A full-size file
took between `r f1(min(syn$seconds))` and `r f1(max(syn$seconds))` seconds to
generate.

```{r tab5}
t5 <- syn
t5$survey_id <- yr4(t5$survey_id)
knitr::kable(t5, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Survey", "Recode", "Indicators calibrated", "Values reproduced", "Records",
                           "Mean absolute deviation", "Largest deviation", "Seconds"),
             caption = "Table 5. Agreement of calibrated synthetic data with the official estimates (percentage points)")
```

```{r fig1, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.2, fig.cap = "Figure 1. Official estimates and the corresponding estimates from calibrated synthetic data, for every calibrated indicator, round and margin. The line marks perfect agreement."}
ggplot(syn_d, aes(official, synthetic)) +
  geom_abline(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Official estimate (%)", y = "Synthetic-data estimate (%)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

## Case study: caesarean delivery, 2004-2022

The share of births delivered by caesarean section rose from
`r f1(cs_at("BD2004DHS"))`% in 2004 to `r f1(cs_at("BD2022DHS"))`% in 2022
(Figure 2). That is an increase of
`r f1(ch("rh_del_csection", "BD2004DHS", "BD2022DHS", "difference"))`
percentage points, or
`r f1(ch("rh_del_csection", "BD2004DHS", "BD2022DHS", "annual_change"), 2)`
points a year, and every change between consecutive rounds was
statistically significant. Facility delivery grew more slowly relative to its
starting level, so that by 2022 about
`r f1(100 * cs_at("BD2022DHS") / fd_at("BD2022DHS"), 0)`% of births in health
facilities were by caesarean section.

```{r fig2, fig.width = 6.2, fig.height = 3.4, fig.cap = "Figure 2. Caesarean and facility delivery among births in the three years before each survey, with 95% confidence intervals."}
yr <- c(BD2000DHS = 2000, BD2004DHS = 2004, BD2007DHS = 2007, BD2011DHS = 2011,
        BD2014DHS = 2014, BD2017DHS = 2018, BD2022DHS = 2022)
d <- trend
d$year <- yr[d$survey_id]
d$what <- ifelse(d$indicator == "rh_del_csection", "Caesarean delivery", "Facility delivery")
ggplot(d, aes(year, estimate, colour = what)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = ci_low, ymax = ci_high), width = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#b2182b", "#2166ac")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Percentage of births", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Absolute inequality by wealth grew as caesarean delivery spread. The slope
index of inequality rose from `r f1(iq("BD2004DHS", "sii"))` percentage
points in 2004 to `r f1(iq("BD2017DHS", "sii"))` in 2017-18 and stood at
`r f1(iq("BD2022DHS", "sii"))` (95% CI `r f1(iq("BD2022DHS", "sii", "ci_low"))`
to `r f1(iq("BD2022DHS", "sii", "ci_high"))`) in 2022. Relative inequality fell
sharply over the same period, from a relative index of
`r f1(iq("BD2004DHS", "rii"), 0)` to `r f1(iq("BD2022DHS", "rii"))`, as women in
the poorest households began to deliver by caesarean section (Table 6). Every
index computed from the microdata agreed closely with the same index derived
from the official estimates by wealth quintile. Erreygers' index in 2022, for
example, was `r f1(iq("BD2022DHS", "eci"), 3)` against
`r f1(iq("BD2022DHS", "eci", "official"), 3)`.

```{r tab6}
t6 <- ineq[ineq$measure %in% c("difference", "sii", "rii", "eci"), c("survey_id", "measure", "estimate")]
t6 <- reshape(t6, idvar = "survey_id", timevar = "measure", direction = "wide")
names(t6) <- sub("estimate.", "", names(t6), fixed = TRUE)
t6$survey_id <- yr4(t6$survey_id)
t6 <- t6[, c("survey_id", "difference", "sii", "rii", "eci")]
knitr::kable(t6, row.names = FALSE, digits = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 3),
             col.names = c("Survey", "Richest minus poorest (points)", "Slope index of inequality",
                           "Relative index of inequality", "Erreygers concentration index"),
             caption = "Table 6. Wealth-related inequality in caesarean delivery")
```

Changes in who was giving birth explained only a small part of the increase
(Table 7). Rising education among mothers accounted for
`r f1(dc("BD2004DHS", "mother_edu_level", "composition"))` of the
`r f1(dc("BD2004DHS", "mother_edu_level", "total"))` percentage-point increase
between 2004 and 2022, or
`r f1(dc("BD2004DHS", "mother_edu_level", "composition", "percent"), 0)`%.
Changes in the wealth distribution accounted for almost none of it
(`r f1(dc("BD2004DHS", "wealth_quintile", "composition", "percent"), 0)`%). The
rest of the increase happened within every education and wealth group.

```{r tab7}
t7 <- dec
t7$period <- paste(sub("BD(\\d{4}).*", "\\1", t7$from), sub("BD(\\d{4}).*", "\\1", t7$to), sep = " to ")
t7$by <- ifelse(t7$by == "mother_edu_level", "Mother's education", "Wealth quintile")
t7$component <- c(composition = "Composition", within = "Within groups", total = "Total change")[t7$component]
knitr::kable(t7[, c("period", "by", "component", "estimate", "se", "percent")], row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Period", "Decomposed by", "Component", "Percentage points", "SE", "Share of change (%)"),
             caption = "Table 7. Decomposition of the change in caesarean delivery")
```

## Progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals

On the official estimates, under-five mortality and child stunting were on
course to meet their 2030 targets (Table 8). Neonatal mortality, wasting and
skilled attendance at birth were not. Child marriage was falling but remained
far from elimination.

```{r tab8}
t8 <- sdg[, c("sdg", "name", "baseline_value", "latest_value", "target", "aarc", "required_aarc", "on_track")]
t8$on_track <- ifelse(is.na(t8$on_track), "–", ifelse(t8$on_track, "Yes", "No"))
knitr::kable(t8, row.names = FALSE, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("SDG", "Indicator", "2014", "2022", "Target", "Annual change (%)",
                           "Required annual change (%)", "On track"),
             caption = "Table 8. Progress towards SDG-related targets, from the official estimates")
```

# Discussion

This study shows that the official BDHS estimates can be reproduced from the
recode files almost exactly, as long as a handful of decisions are made
correctly. Once the survey design, denominators, reference periods and
round-specific rules were written down in code, `r n_pass` of `r n_val`
national estimates matched the published values, most of them to within a
few hundredths of a percentage point. Inequality measures computed from the
microdata also agreed with those derived from the official tables. The same
exercise showed that the decisions that matter most are ones the data files
do not reveal.

The largest errors come from how the sample was drawn, not from the
statistical method. Because every BDHS women's sample is limited to women who
have ever been married, child marriage estimated without all-woman factors
comes out about ten percentage points too high. Bangladesh's child-marriage
problem is serious enough without overstating it. In 2022 the error runs the
other way: counting women who were never asked about family planning as having
no unmet need understates it by a third, and would suggest much faster
progress since 2017-18 than actually took place.

Other conventions matter less but are still worth getting right. Some are
documented only implicitly, in the way the official tables were produced. The
child-marriage tables use the total all-woman factor for every subgroup,
while the subgroup factors are used elsewhere. The exclusive breastfeeding
indicator leaves out the country-specific liquids that the questionnaire
records. Neither choice can be inferred from the data documentation alone,
and each moves estimates by more than their sampling error.

Design effects of `r f1(min(deff$deff))` to `r f1(max(deff$deff))` are typical of
DHS surveys but are still often ignored. Treating the BDHS as a simple random
sample makes estimates look more precise than they are, which matters most
when comparing subgroups or rounds. Regional comparisons over time raise a
further, practical problem: because divisions were renumbered when Mymensingh
division was created, the same code refers to different places in different
rounds. Any regional trend analysis needs harmonised division boundaries.

The data-quality assessment is mostly reassuring. Birth histories are
complete, and there is no sign of the displacement of births out of the
health-question window that distorts estimates in some DHS countries.
Anthropometric measurement improved markedly after 2011, which supports the
comparability of recent nutrition estimates. Three patterns deserve
attention, and all are consistent with earlier assessments of age and date
reporting in DHS surveys [@pullum2006]:

- height-for-age z-scores remain more dispersed than expected, which may
  slightly inflate stunting estimates;
- the heaping of deaths at 12 months moves some deaths between the infant and
  child mortality intervals;
- the shortage of women recorded at age 50 relative to 49 points to age
  misreporting at the edge of eligibility for the women's interview.

The calibrated synthetic data meet a practical need. Because DHS files cannot
be shared, the analysis code in published papers usually cannot be run by
readers, students practise on toy data, and new methods are hard to
demonstrate. Synthetic files that reproduce the published national and
regional estimates let worked examples behave like the real survey without
containing information about any respondent. They suit teaching, software
testing and reproducible demonstrations. They should not be used for
substantive conclusions, because the associations between indicators are not
reproduced.

The case study shows how the tools work together. Caesarean delivery in
Bangladesh rose roughly ten-fold in less than two decades, part of a rapid
global increase [@betran2016]. As its use spread beyond the richest
households, absolute inequality widened while relative inequality fell.
Changes in maternal education and household wealth explain only a small part
of the rise, which occurred within every group. That pattern points to changes
in health-system practice rather than in the characteristics of the mothers.
Separating these components with proper standard errors is straightforward
once the design and indicator definitions are right.

bdhs complements existing tools rather than replacing them. IPUMS-DHS remains
the better choice for comparisons between countries with harmonised variables
[@ipumsdhs], and rdhs and DHS.rates serve every DHS country [@watson2019;
@dhsrates]. bdhs reproduces DHS.rates exactly for the rates both packages
compute. Its contribution is depth for one country: every round, the original
files, validation against the official estimates, and Bangladesh-specific
harmonisation and documentation.

The study has limitations. Validation was limited to the recode files
available to the author, mainly the children's recodes for the earlier
rounds, with complete sets only for 2017-18 and 2022. No files from 1996-97
were available, and its harmonisation rules, taken from the published
codebook, remain unverified. A tolerance of half a percentage point for
national estimates does not guarantee agreement for every subgroup, although
the subgroup comparisons we made agreed closely. The synthetic data reproduce
only the calibrated values. Finally, the package does not yet produce
estimates below the division level, which are increasingly needed for
planning.

# Conclusions

Analyses of the BDHS can reproduce the official estimates almost exactly.
Doing so depends on handling the ever-married samples, questionnaire changes,
country-specific conventions and survey design correctly; getting them wrong
shifts key indicators by up to ten percentage points. Writing these decisions
down once, in validated and openly available software, makes BDHS analyses
more accurate, quicker to carry out and easier to check. We suggest that
analyses of DHS data routinely report how their national estimates compare
with the official figures.

# List of abbreviations

AARC: average annual rate of change; BDHS: Bangladesh Demographic and Health
Survey; CI: confidence interval; DHS: Demographic and Health Surveys; GFR:
general fertility rate; KR, IR, PR, BR, HR: children's, individual (women's),
household-member, births and household recode files; NIPORT: National
Institute of Population Research and Training; RII: relative index of
inequality; SD: standard deviation; SDG: Sustainable Development Goal; SE:
standard error; SII: slope index of inequality.
